title: Franchise Disclosure Document: The 14-Day Rule and How to Manage It
description: Korean franchisors must provide the disclosure document 14 days before signing. Learn the risks, why proof of viewing matters and how to keep a reliable record.
html:
The duty to provide the franchise disclosure document in advance: the 14-day rule and how to manage it

The statutory period for pre-disclosure documents is counted from the date of delivery

CORE SUMMARY

✓ The franchise disclosure document must be provided to a prospective franchisee at least 14 days before the franchise contract is signed.

✓ Missing this period can give grounds for a claim to refund franchise fees.

✓ For HQ, the practical crux is whether it can prove when, to whom and which documents it provided.

✓ Individual cases should be assessed against Korea Fair Trade Commission standards and with legal counsel.

The duty to provide the franchise disclosure document in advance requires a franchisor to provide the disclosure document, a document on nearby franchise stores and related materials to a prospective franchisee for a set period before signing a franchise contract. It is a procedure set out in Korea's Fair Transactions in Franchise Business Act (the Franchise Business Act), designed to give prospective franchisees enough time to review the contract terms.

For HQ, this duty isn't just about handing over paperwork. You can only say you truly complied if you can prove when you provided the documents. This article covers the key standards of the pre-disclosure duty and how HQ should manage it in practice.

What is the duty to provide the franchise disclosure document in advance?

Pre-disclosure must happen a set period before the contract is signed

The Franchise Business Act provides that a franchisor may sign a franchise contract or receive franchise fees only after 14 days have passed since it provided the disclosure document to the prospective franchisee. This period is the minimum time guaranteed for the prospective franchisee to review the disclosure document and, if needed, visit existing stores or seek professional advice.

So complying with the pre-disclosure duty doesn't just mean the document was delivered. It means keeping a record showing that the delivery date came at least 14 days before the contract date.

The risks of failing the pre-disclosure duty

If the delivery date is unclear, HQ is at a disadvantage in any later dispute

Confirmed risk

If a franchisor receives franchise fees without providing the disclosure document, or without observing the statutory period, the prospective franchisee has grounds to claim a refund of those fees. However, the specific criteria and procedures vary by case, so individual application should be confirmed against Korea Fair Trade Commission standards and with legal counsel.

In practice, most problems stem not from the violation itself but from proof. Even if the document was clearly delivered, without a record proving when, HQ will struggle to justify itself in a dispute.

Why HQ needs to be able to prove pre-disclosure history

An email outbox or text history alone can hardly prove that a document was actually opened

Many franchisors deliver the disclosure document by email or in print and rely on a personal mailbox or a staffer's memory as the only record of sending it. But if the delivery date later becomes an issue, proof of sending alone makes it hard to show when the recipient actually viewed it.

Delivery and viewing are different facts. HQ's position in a later dispute is far clearer if its records include not just the fact that the document was sent, but also the date and time the prospective franchisee viewed it.

Building a structure that leaves a record from pre-disclosure to contract

You need a structure where sending, viewing and contracting connect into a single record

As a franchise-specialist software developer with GS (Good Software) certification, we've seen how many headquarters manage contracts. The difference between those that reliably manage the pre-disclosure duty and those that don't ultimately comes down to whether records stay in a system or in people's memories.

Because the send time and view time are kept for each lead, you can confirm whether the 14-day standard was met without relying on anyone's memory. What's often missed in managing disclosure documents

The completeness of the record is missed more often than the document itself

Delivery date recordAre you recording not just the send date but the view date?
14-day countAre you automatically counting back from the contract date to check the period?
Nearby store documentIs there a separate record that it was provided with the disclosure document?
Contract renewal timingDo you know in advance which contracts are about to expire?

Frequently asked questions

Q. Exactly how long is the pre-disclosure period?

Under the Franchise Business Act, a franchise contract may be signed and franchise fees received only after 14 days have passed since the disclosure document was provided. Specific exceptions should be confirmed against Korea Fair Trade Commission standards.

Q. Is a record of emailing the disclosure document enough?

A sending record alone makes it hard to prove when the recipient actually viewed it. A method that also records the view date and time gives HQ stronger evidence in any later dispute.

Q. Why is the contract expiration alert set at 30 days?

It secures the minimum practical time needed to discuss renewal and prepare re-contracting documents. If you only find out right before expiration, there isn't enough time to negotiate.

Q. What should we do if a dispute over the disclosure document arises?

Make your case based on the delivery and viewing records HQ holds, but confirm the specific course of action through Korea Fair Trade Commission procedures and legal counsel.

The pre-disclosure duty ultimately comes down to whether you can prove the timing. When HQ keeps records in a system, meeting the statutory period stops being a separate task to track and becomes a procedure that's verified naturally.
